doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

chapter: Teaching and spread of New Orleans jazz
title: Worldwide players of New Orleans style jazz
summary: White lists devoted players in Japan, Europe and elsewhere, and says the Bunk Johnson and George Lewis revival was the biggest influence.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well yeah, and also I mean just the fact that a lot of later generation people, you know, you like the music of your generation or whatever, and a lot of people just didn’t respect it ‘cause it was old, or they didn’t respect it because they didn’t think it was hip. You know they didn’t use as many scales and altered things and it wasn’t, in general, as fast and technical. You know it presented a different kind of challenge. It wasn’t something that you could sit down and say analyze and say this is this scale and you practice this for so many hours, months – weeks, months – and you can come out and play it on the job and people think you’re raising hell. It’s – how do you play from the soul? How do you develop a real, genuine, original self-expression, and how do you do that in collective improvisation? How do you create while other people are creating collectively to create a tapestry that’s greater than any one individual. Yeah, that’s hard to teach. However, I mean and in this country it has a lot of different implications, some of which are racial implications and all this, but there are people, no matter what anybody says, there are people all over the world of all ages and all nationalities that play authentic New Orleans style jazz. They’re not necessarily going to schools to learn it, they learn it from listening to records and getting with people in places like in Japan, the second largest university there, Waseda University, there’s a New Orleans jazz club that started in the 1960s as a result of George Lewis’s first three month tour there, and they have several bands of musicians. Some of the musicians are deceased now, a number of them are older than me, and they still have kids, you know 18, 19 years old learning this music, come over to New Orleans, they sound so much like the early musicians ‘til it’s frightening. But there are people all over Europe, all over Scandinavia, you know Norway, Sweden, Finland, France, England, Germany, Australia playing this music, Canada. And you know some of the younger people that I see, it’s refreshing to hear them because some of them, you know people always say, “Oh well they’re just copying what somebody else played.” Some people were, but there are a lot of people now playing this music creatively. Because they understand that there are a set of musical principles that can be used to endless creation, or at least for developing your own original style and you know you can have a mentor or an idol that you sound something like, but you know when I went to Morocco the trombone player was a young lady from Japan who now lives in New

Orleans and she sounds more like the authentic trombone style than most people in New Orleans today you know. There’s a guy, a young guy from Canada, Toronto, who moved to New Orleans and he plays bass and he sounds like the old bass players. He sounds like Chester Zardis and Bill Johnson and Al Morgan you know and all these people. But he’s very creative you know. And so that’s – the way I feel about the music, I’m finding that some of these younger people all over the world feel the same way that you can play this music and be yourself. And they are not learning in school, and they are not having people, you know, some of them never get to New Orleans, some of them come to New Orleans, some of them move to New Orleans. So, but there have been people playing this music all along. The music of the 1920s had some influence and in some places you see people trying to play like King Oliver. Of course in France there were a lot of people trying to replicate Sidney Bechet’s music. But what probably had the biggest impact was the New Orleans revival, Bunk Johnson and George Lewis. And so the majority of bands I hear from other places are influenced by that. You know George Lewis’s band, Kid Thomas Valentine, people like that. And again, it varies. You have some people that are, you know, copying and imitating, and other people that are creative in the style.
